reply: {"summary": "CtRL-Sim controls agent behaviour by exponentially tilting the learned return distribution. For each reward dimension c a coefficient kappa_c is set (evaluated from -25 to 25); negative tilting yields worse-than-average behaviour, positive tilting better-than-average, and metrics change relatively monotonically with kappa. Fine-tuning on only 3500 CAT collision scenarios (30 minutes on one A100) strengthens adversarial behaviour: at -25 tilting the fine-tuned model produces 2.1x the collisions and 1.8x the offroad violations of the base model; at -10 it yields 238 more planner collisions over 1000 scenes. CAT makes more collisions but is not controllable and its agents are non-reactive.", "relevance_score": 9}

{"summary": "Scenario Diffusion is a latent diffusion model whose controllability comes from conditioning. Map conditioning: a BEV map image is encoded and concatenated with the noisy sample along channels. Token conditioning: tokens enter the denoiser through cross-attention. Agent tokens are procedurally computed per agent (position, speed, length, motion profile). Partial tokenization with a mask probability p_mask lets the model generate agents without tokens. A global scene token encodes p_mask and controls the number of agents at inference; no agent tokens with p_mask=1 gives map-only generation.", "relevance_score": 9}

{"summary": "A guided VAE builds control into the latent space instead of external conditioning, which the authors say can distort the underlying probability distribution (critical for failure-probability estimation). One latent dimension encodes the scenario class: z=[z_type, z_rest], with a class-conditional prior N(z_type|mu_y, sigma_y^2) times N(z_rest|0,I) and an alignment loss pulling z_type to the class centre; total loss is reconstruction plus beta*KL plus alignment. Data: about 44,600 highway trajectories of six scenario types (cut-in, cut-out, cut-through, left and right). Validation classification error is at most 2e-2.", "relevance_score": 8}

{"summary": "DragTraffic generates future trajectories conditioned on a context that can include vehicle type, length and width, starting position, speed and orientation, and target position, speed and orientation. For editing existing scenarios the target state is the condition; for new scenarios the initial agent states come from dragging, typing or an agent placement module. A MultiPath++ regression model gives an initial trajectory, and a conditional diffusion model refines it. CTG uses conditional diffusion for controllable simulation and CTG++ adds language instructions, but such methods need expert-designed constraints and loss functions.", "relevance_score": 8}

{"summary": "DragTraffic's interaction-reasoning table reports a metric labelled SCR(%) that is lower with user conditions: 9.20 versus 15.00 at a 3 s rollout and 3.33 versus 13.59 at 9 s, against a mixture-training baseline with condition. In a case study, setting condition information for agent 1 (100 m ahead, longitudinal speed 20 m/s, lateral speed -2 m/s) removes a robot-freezing behaviour. Control of several agents is possible at once and needs only dragging or typing, not complex optimization constraints or loss design. The conclusion says user context enters the denoising process via cross-attention.", "relevance_score": 7}

{"summary": "DragTraffic is an instance-behaviour-level traffic scene generator aimed at high controllability. A regression model gives initial guesses, a symmetric hybrid expert (mixture of experts) architecture uses a separate model per agent type, and a conditional diffusion model, inspired by DragGAN, provides diversity and honours specified context: position, velocity, heading, length and width. Controls are applied by dragging or typing. The authors contrast this with CTG++, which needs repeated and complex training for different tasks, and claim the first interactive framework with this freedom for generating and editing traffic scenes.", "relevance_score": 7}

{"summary": "DragTraffic abstract: a generalized, interactive, controllable traffic scene generation framework based on conditional diffusion, with an adaptive mixture-of-experts architecture for different agent types, a regression model for the initial solution and diffusion refinement for diversity; user-customized context enters through cross-attention. The introduction argues prior methods lack controllability: many treat scene generation as motion prediction needing 10 frames of history, which limits editing and agent insertion, and two-stage methods such as SceneGen and TrafficGen lack controllability.", "relevance_score": 6}

{"summary": "In the Scenario Dreamer appendix, the CtRL-Sim behaviour model is evaluated with exponentially tilted behaviour, kappa=+10 (positive) and kappa=-50 (negative). Positive tilting gives the lowest planner collision rate (4.9%); negative tilting keeps realistic behaviour with only a modest rise in JSD metrics while the planner collision rate rises by 7 percentage points, without fine-tuning on adversarial data. Scenario Dreamer itself supports lane-conditioned object generation, initial scene generation and inpainting, and scenes can be generated conditioned on a fixed number of lanes (24) and agents (8).", "relevance_score": 6}

{"summary": "ControlNeXt targets image and video diffusion, not driving. It injects control signals with a lightweight convolution module, freezes most base-model parameters and trains a small subset, and replaces zero-convolution with Cross Normalization, cutting learnable parameters by up to 90%. Only loosely related as a general controllable-diffusion technique.", "relevance_score": 2}
